paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists treated kinship as the cultural elaboration of a biological given: every society, on this view, recognized ties of procreation, and what varied was the use each made of them, which links it counted, which it ignored, and what duties it attached to each. The critique that gathered force in the 1970s held that this framework smuggled a Euro-American folk theory into comparison. If some peoples reckoned relatedness through shared food, shared land or long co-residence rather than through birth, then to call their categories kinship at all was to measure them against a standard they did not share.

The critique was salutary, but its most radical conclusion, that kinship should be abandoned as a comparative category, has not survived the ethnography it inspired. Studies of relatedness in Southeast Asia and Amazonia found that people who insist that kin are made, through feeding and propinquity, do not therefore think birth irrelevant; they treat it as one way, often the first, in which a tie begins, and expect the tie to be confirmed or to lapse according to what follows. Nor were the obligations that mediated these ties less binding for being acquired: a foster child who had eaten from a household's hearth for years could be obligated to it as firmly as any offspring. What the newer work demarcates, then, is not a domain in which biology plays no part but one in which it is not privileged, and that is a finding comparison can accommodate, provided the comparison begins from what people do to become related rather than from a presumed genealogical grid.

Of the signals that precede an eruption, the swelling of a volcano's flanks has long seemed the most legible: magma rising into a shallow reservoir pushes the ground upward, and instruments that register a few centimeters of uplift can betray an intrusion to which an observer standing on the summit would be wholly oblivious. Yet uplift alone portends less than it appears to. Many reservoirs inflate and deflate for decades without erupting, and at some volcanoes eruptions have begun after little measurable swelling, because magma can rise through a conduit left open by earlier activity without having to pry the surrounding rock apart. For this reason observatories increasingly read deformation alongside the chemistry of escaping gas: a rising proportion of sulfur dioxide relative to carbon dioxide, which escapes from magma at greater depths, indicates that the magma is shallow and actively degassing, a palpable warning even when the ground itself is still.

Because Bach's last contrapuntal cycle was printed in open score, each voice on its own staff, and names no instrument, it was long held up as the paradigmatic instance of music for the eye: a compendium of fugal technique to be studied rather than heard, and so, in the judgment of one nineteenth-century editor, beyond the reach of any performance. The reading flattered a certain metaphysical image of the composer as an aging polymath withdrawn from the world into pure number, and it made the cycle's occasional awkward passages easy to excuse as the price of demonstration.

The case against that reading was built by scholars who interrogated the notes themselves. Nearly every voice lies within the compass of a keyboard of the period, and, more tellingly, the combinations hardest to disentangle on the page almost always fall comfortably under two hands, as though each had been tried at the instrument. Open score, moreover, proved nothing about abstraction: it was the customary way of printing learned counterpoint, adopted so that a student could follow each line, not a sign that the lines were never meant to sound together.

Yet the revisionists' victory has been more complete than their evidence. To show that the cycle can be played at a keyboard is not to show that it was conceived for one alone; writing that suits two hands may suit a consort of viols as well, and a composer who habitually rearranged his own works for new forces may not have thought the question worth settling. What the keyboard argument does establish is narrower and, in its way, more interesting: that the cycle was meant to be sounded, by whatever means, and that its difficulties are not the residue of a demonstration but problems the composer expected performers to solve, each of whom might inflect the solution differently.

Few features of Byzantine icons have invited more theorizing than their so-called inverse perspective: tables and footstools that widen as they recede, buildings whose two sides are visible at once. Early in the twentieth century a group of writers, several of them priests, argued that the device was deliberate, a refusal of mimetic illusion meant to open the depicted space toward the worshiper rather than away from him, so that the icon became less a window onto a scene than a threshold across which the numinous advanced. The argument is attractive, and it has the merit of taking seriously what icons were for. But it credits painters with a reasoned rejection of a system, linear perspective, that few of them could have known, and it passes over the awkward fact that the convergences within a single icon are rarely consistent: one object may widen toward the back while its neighbor narrows. A painter who meant to invert perspective would presumably have inverted it throughout. The inconsistency more plausibly records a workshop habit that subordinated the coherence of the whole space to the legibility of each object, tilting a table's top toward the viewer so that the book lying on it could be seen. None of this nullifies the theologians' insight that the habit served devotion; what the icons themselves do little to confirm is that it was devised to limn a theology of space.

When a volcano erupts after its warnings have gone unheeded, the failure is commonly laid at the door of the forecast: scientists, it is said, could not say when the eruption would come, and officials, handed an uncertain warning, declined to order an evacuation whose costs were certain. On this view the remedy is better science, denser networks of instruments and sharper models, until warnings become precise enough to compel action.

The historical record supports a less comfortable reading. In some of the deadliest eruptions of the past century the hazard was not in doubt: maps drawn weeks beforehand showed which valleys a mudflow would follow, and the towns in its path were named. What was missing was not knowledge but a nexus between those who possessed it and those empowered to act, for the scientists reported to one ministry and civil defense to another, factious rivals each of which could plausibly regard the decision as the other's. Greater precision would not have closed that gap; in more than one case a specific warning arrived on the day itself and was never relayed. An evacuation called too early does exact a price, since it can leave residents insouciant about the next one and so jeopardize it; still, the decisive variable in such disasters has often been institutional rather than scientific. Observatories that have absorbed the lesson now rehearse evacuations with the agencies that would order them, treating the chain of communication as part of the forecast itself.

Two years ago the town of Brask began requiring every restaurant that opens or remodels a kitchen to install a grease trap and to have it inspected each quarter. Since then, the number of sewer blockages reported in Brask has fallen by nearly half, while in the neighboring town of Holm, which imposes no such requirement, the number has held steady. Brask's public works director concludes that the inspection requirement is chiefly responsible for the decline.

Last year the municipal pool in Corwin extended its hours, staying open until ten at night instead of closing at six. Over the year, the total number of swimmer visits rose by 30 percent, yet the number of incidents in which a lifeguard had to rescue a swimmer fell by nearly a third.

questions.prompt: The painter's late canvases are remarkable above all for their ___: a single stroke stands for a sleeve, and a bare patch of linen does the work of the glare off water.

explanation.key: One stroke for a sleeve and bare linen for glare are the fewest possible means doing the most work: economy, in its secondary sense of careful, sparing use of means (not the everyday 'the economy').

distractors.profusion: Abundance; the examples show the opposite, a minimum of marks.
distractors.opulence: Lavish richness; bare linen is anything but.
distractors.bravura: Showy virtuosity; the examples stress restraint, not display.
distractors.ambiguity: The stroke clearly 'stands for a sleeve'; nothing is left uncertain.

questions.prompt: Jurors who took the witness's (i) ___ manner for indifference were mistaken. Her earlier testimony shows the same flat calm even when she described her own injuries, and her physician later explained that years of illness had taught her to be (ii) ___ about pain.

explanation.key: (i) A 'flat calm' that jurors misread as indifference is an emotionless manner: impassive. (ii) Years of illness taught her to bear pain without complaint or display: stoic.

distractors.histrionic: Theatrical emotion is the opposite of flat calm.
distractors.truculent: Aggressive defiance would not be mistaken for indifference.
distractors.querulous: Complaining is the opposite of what the flat calm shows.
distractors.squeamish: Easily upset; she described her injuries calmly.

questions.prompt: Readers who took the ombudsman's report as a (i) ___ of the agency, on the strength of its confirmation that the delays were real, misread it: the report held that it was (ii) ___ on the legislature, not on the agency, to provide the funds that would clear the backlog, and it was careful to (iii) ___ its tally of missed deadlines by noting how steeply caseloads had risen.

explanation.key: The reading that a confirmation of real delays would invite is a reprimand, and the colon says that reading is wrong because the report shifts responsibility and softens its findings. (i) censure (formal disapproval). (ii) 'it was ___ on the legislature, not on the agency, to provide the funds' assigns a duty: incumbent (obligatory), not the everyday 'current officeholder'. (iii) Noting rising caseloads moderates the sting of the tally: temper.

distractors.vindication: Confirming that the delays were real gives no ground for reading the report as a vindication; that reading would not be 'on the strength of' the confirmation.
distractors.travesty: A grotesque misrepresentation; nothing about confirming the delays would lead readers to take the report as a distortion of the agency.
distractors.onerous: Burdensome does not assign responsibility, so it cannot carry the contrast 'on the legislature, not on the agency'.
distractors.lenient: 'Lenient on the legislature ... to provide the funds' is not grammatical and assigns no duty.
distractors.compound: To worsen; noting caseloads is a mitigating context, and the report is lenient toward the agency.
distractors.belie: To show to be false; rising caseloads explain the missed deadlines but do not contradict the tally.

questions.prompt: Translators who had found the philosopher's German impenetrable were surprised by her English lectures, whose ___ style let undergraduates follow arguments that had defeated specialists in the original.

explanation.key: The surprise is the contrast with 'impenetrable', and the result is that beginners could follow the arguments: the style was transparently clear. Pellucid and perspicuous.

distractors.grandiloquent: Trap pair with bombastic: true synonyms for pompous, inflated prose, which would not let undergraduates follow hard arguments.
distractors.bombastic: Trap pair with grandiloquent: wrong polarity.
distractors.elliptical: Leaving things out, hard to follow; the opposite of the surprise.
distractors.arcane: Understood only by a few; that describes the German, not the lectures.

questions.prompt: Reviewers who expected a soldier's memoir to be padded with campaign trivia found it ___ instead: in under two hundred pages it covered four wars, and its one-sentence verdicts on his generals became the most quoted lines of the decade.

explanation.key: 'Instead' of padding, the memoir covers four wars in under two hundred pages with one-sentence verdicts: brief and pointed. Laconic and succinct.

distractors.garrulous: Trap pair with loquacious: true synonyms for talkative, the padding the reviewers expected.
distractors.loquacious: Trap pair with garrulous: the expectation the sentence overturns.
distractors.evasive: His verdicts on the generals were quotable precisely because they were direct.

questions.prompt: Her columns were admired for a wit that was ___ without ever being cruel: she could puncture an argument's pretensions in a sentence while leaving its author's dignity intact.

explanation.key: Wit that punctures pretensions but is not cruel is sharp and biting yet controlled: mordant and astringent.

distractors.saccharine: Trap pair with cloying: true synonyms for overly sweet, the opposite of wit that punctures.
distractors.cloying: Trap pair with saccharine: wrong polarity.
distractors.rancorous: Bitter and spiteful: that is the cruelty the sentence says she avoided.
distractors.insipid: Bland; bland wit could not puncture anything.

questions.prompt: The witness who had stonewalled the committee for three days became surprisingly ___ once he was granted immunity, volunteering names and dates the investigators had not even asked for.

explanation.key: After stonewalling, he 'volunteered' more than was asked: he became open and willing to tell. Forthcoming (secondary sense, willing to give information) and candid.

distractors.guarded: Trap pair with taciturn: both describe the close-mouthed witness before immunity.
distractors.taciturn: Trap pair with guarded: the state he left behind.
distractors.mendacious: Lying; nothing says his volunteered names were false.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend the genealogical model of kinship against a critique that charged it with importing a Euro-American folk theory into comparison
argue that the most sweeping conclusion drawn from a critique outran the evidence that the critique itself helped to produce
show that ethnographic studies of relatedness confirmed the critique's claim that birth plays no part in how many peoples reckon kinship
explain why peoples in Southeast Asia and Amazonia reckon relatedness through feeding and co-residence rather than through birth
propose that comparative studies of kinship be replaced by studies of how particular peoples become related

explanation.key: The passage calls the critique salutary but says its radical conclusion (abandon kinship as a comparative category) 'has not survived the ethnography it inspired': the critique's own offspring evidence undercuts its strongest claim.

distractors.defend the genealogical model of kinship: Wrong verb: the author calls the critique salutary and ends by rejecting a 'presumed genealogical grid'.
distractors.show that ethnographic studies of relate: Reversed: the studies found that these peoples do not think birth irrelevant.
distractors.explain why peoples in Southeast Asia an: Too narrow and distorted: the passage reports how, not why, and says birth still counts.
distractors.propose that comparative studies of kins: The author keeps comparison and only changes its starting point; 'replaced' is the radical conclusion the passage rejects.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage suggests which of the following about the peoples described in the studies of relatedness?
choices: They treat a tie that begins at birth as one whose standing depends in part on what happens afterward.
Their ways of reckoning relatedness were among those that first prompted anthropologists to question the genealogical model.
They could count as kin a person to whom they have no tie of birth while ceasing to count as kin a person to whom they have one.

explanation.key: A: correct; birth is one way a tie begins, and they 'expect the tie to be confirmed or to lapse according to what follows'. B: unsupported; the studies are 'the ethnography it inspired', so they came after the critique rather than prompting it. C: correct by combining two sentences: an acquired tie (the foster child fed at the hearth) can bind as firmly as birth, and a tie begun at birth can lapse, so both halves are possible.

questions.prompt: In the context in which it appears, "legible" most nearly means

explanation.key: Swelling 'has long seemed the most legible' of the signals, yet 'uplift alone portends less than it appears to': it seemed easy to read meaning from, which is the claim the passage then qualifies. Legible here means easily interpreted.

distractors.readily measured: The trap: uplift is readily measured (instruments register a few centimeters), but the passage's 'Yet' turns on what uplift means, not on whether it can be measured; measurability is never put in doubt.
distractors.clearly printed: The everyday sense of legible (handwriting or type); no text is involved.
distractors.carefully recorded: Recording is the instruments' job; legibility concerns reading the record's meaning.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that identifies something left by a volcano's earlier activity that can reduce the warning its ground gives before an eruption.

explanation.key: The third sentence (Many reservoirs inflate and deflate ...) states that magma can rise through 'a conduit left open by earlier activity' without prying the rock apart, so an eruption may follow little swelling. The last sentence mentions a still ground but names nothing left by earlier activity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?
choices: Brask's sewer lines are, on average, newer than Holm's.
Restaurants in Brask whose grease traps are inspected report fewer plumbing problems in their own kitchens than restaurants whose traps are not.
Over the past two years, more than four-fifths of Brask's restaurants have either opened new kitchens or remodeled existing ones.
Two years ago Brask also began a campaign urging residents not to pour cooking fat down household drains.
Holm has more restaurants per resident than Brask has.

explanation.key: The requirement applies only to kitchens that open or remodel. If few did, it could not explain a near-halving of blockages. Showing that more than four-fifths of restaurants came under the rule closes that gap.

distractors.Restaurants in Brask whose grease traps: Supports a different conclusion (traps help restaurants' own plumbing), not that the rule cut town sewer blockages.
distractors.Two years ago Brask also began a campaig: Weakens: it offers a rival cause for the decline.
distractors.Holm has more restaurants per resident t: Bears on Holm's level of blockages, not on what changed in Brask.
distractors.Brask's sewer lines are, on average, new: A standing difference between the towns; it cannot explain a change in Brask over the past two years, and says nothing about the requirement.

questions.prompt: His admirers took the dealer's having bought the icons for a pittance and resold them within the year at twenty times the price as evidence of his ___; his detractors, without disputing the figures, noted that the estate sale at which he had bought them was advertised only in a parish newsletter that he himself edited.

explanation.key: Admirers read the profit as a credit to him: keen business judgment, acumen. The detractors accept the figures but hint that he rigged the sale, recasting the same facts as something less creditable.

distractors.probity: Honesty has nothing to do with buying cheap and selling dear, and the detractors' point would attack it only if admirers had claimed it.
distractors.guile: This is the detractors' insinuation (cunning deceit), not what admirers would call him.
distractors.frugality: Thrift explains buying cheaply but not the praised resale at twenty times the price.
distractors.largesse: Generosity is the opposite of profiting on a resale.

questions.prompt: Because both governments had already carried out the treaty's terms, the vote to (i) ___ it, a formality the treaty's supporters had demanded so that the agreement would at last carry the force of law, was widely regarded as (ii) ___: whatever the legislators decided, the border would not move.

explanation.key: (i) A formality that gives an agreement 'the force of law' is formal approval: ratify. (ii) Since the terms were already carried out and 'the border would not move' whatever the outcome, the vote had no practical consequence: moot, in its secondary sense, not 'open to debate'.

distractors.repudiate: Supporters would not demand a vote to reject the treaty.
distractors.draft: The treaty already existed and had been carried out; it needed approval, not drafting.
distractors.decisive: The colon says the vote decided nothing.
distractors.premature: The terms had already been carried out, so the vote came late, not early.

questions.prompt: What made the cross-examination a model of (i) ___ was, paradoxically, that no single question in it was deceptive: each was harmless on its face, and the witness, answering freely, did not see that the very point he had come to deny was already (ii) ___ in his answers until the last question stated it outright, a revelation that (iii) ___ him more than any hostile question could have.

explanation.key: The paradox: no question deceived, yet the sequence trapped the witness, so the craft lay in the arrangement: (i) guile. He did not see the point in his own answers until the last question made it explicit, so it was there (ii) implicit, unstated but present. Discovering this disconcerted him: (iii) discomfited.

distractors.candor: The bait: 'no single question was deceptive' suggests frankness, but the series as a whole led the witness into a trap.
distractors.prolixity: Wordiness is not what made the questioning effective.
distractors.exonerated: The revelation hurt his position; it did not clear him.
distractors.invigorated: Wrong polarity: the revelation unsettled him.
distractors.emphatic: A point stated emphatically is one he would have noticed; the final question had to state it outright.
distractors.absent: If the point were absent from his answers, stating it would reveal nothing about him.

questions.prompt: Critics who found the poet's late verse (i) ___, forever lecturing its readers on virtue, also complained of its (ii) ___ diction, crowded with words that had dropped out of speech a century earlier; but the moralizing, at least, is no (iii) ___ in her career, since the juvenilia she published at nineteen preach just as insistently.

explanation.key: (i) 'Forever lecturing its readers on virtue' = didactic. (ii) Words that dropped out of speech a century earlier = archaic. (iii) The early poems preach too, so the late moralizing is not a departure from her norm: no anomaly. 'At least' implies the diction may be.

distractors.derivative: Imitative; the gloss that follows is about lecturing, not borrowing.
distractors.colloquial: Conversational diction is the opposite of words long gone from speech.
distractors.florid: Ornate is a different fault; the gloss specifies obsolete words, not ornament.
distractors.constant: Reversed: juvenilia that preach just as insistently show the moralizing is a constant.
distractors.asset: Whether the moralizing helps her has nothing to do with whether it was already present at nineteen.

questions.prompt: What made the conductor's programs seem ___ was not that they lacked a principle but that the principle, to perform whatever his predecessor had neglected, was one no subscriber could have guessed.

explanation.key: 'Not that they lacked a principle' gives the usual reason for the appearance in question: the word must mean governed by whim rather than system. Arbitrary and capricious do.

distractors.derivative: Trap pair with imitative: copying the predecessor is the reverse of performing what he neglected.
distractors.imitative: Trap pair with derivative: same failure.
distractors.esoteric: The bait: neglected works might seem obscure, but obscurity is not something one would explain away by 'not that they lacked a principle'.
distractors.austere: Severe or plain; nothing in the sentence concerns spareness, and lacking a principle does not explain it.

questions.prompt: Admirers called the poet's late fragments ___, as if what they withheld were a secret; her editor, who had seen the drafts, knew that they withheld nothing but the revisions she had stopped making.

explanation.key: The admirers' word treats the fragments' gaps as concealing a meaning: mysterious, hard to interpret. Enigmatic and inscrutable both fit.

distractors.slipshod: Pair with perfunctory: careless is the editor's verdict, not the admirers'.
distractors.perfunctory: Pair with slipshod: done without care, again the editor's view.
distractors.lapidary: Trap pair with pithy: concise and polished is praise for fragments but says nothing about withholding a secret.
distractors.pithy: Trap pair with lapidary: brief and forceful, not mysterious.

questions.prompt: Those who dismissed the movement as ___ were wrong about its fate but right about its temperament: it outlived every rival school, yet its painters, as solemn as any academician, never chose a subject other than the passing moment.

explanation.key: The dismissive word must make a prediction about fate (refuted by its long life) and also describe its temperament (a devotion to the passing moment, pursued solemnly). Ephemeral and evanescent (fleeting) do both.

distractors.frivolous: Trap pair with trifling: a dismissive word, but it predicts nothing about the movement's fate, and 'as solemn as any academician' rules it out even on temperament.
distractors.trifling: Trap pair with frivolous: same failure; solemn painters are not trifling.
distractors.archaic: Fails both: it predicts nothing about fate, and a movement celebrating the passing moment is not old-fashioned in temperament.
distractors.derivative: A charge about originality, unrelated to fate or to the passing moment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A view is described together with an account of its appeal; the evidence that displaced it is summarized; the conclusion drawn from that evidence is judged broader than the evidence warrants, and a more limited conclusion is drawn.
A view is described together with an account of its appeal; the evidence that displaced it is summarized and found inconclusive; the original view is then partly restored.
Two rival views are described; the evidence for each is weighed; a compromise combining elements of both is proposed.
A view is described and its origins traced; the evidence against it is summarized; the author argues that this evidence has been neglected by later scholars.
A view is described together with an account of its appeal; the evidence that displaced it is summarized; that evidence is then extended to show that the cycle was written for a consort of viols.

explanation.key: Paragraph 1: the 'music for the eye' reading and why it flattered. Paragraph 2: the keyboard evidence. Paragraph 3: the revisionists' victory 'more complete than their evidence', and a 'narrower' claim (meant to be sounded) that the evidence does establish.

distractors.A view is described together with an acc: One move off: the author does not restore the 'music for the eye' view; the narrower claim (meant to be sounded) rejects it.
distractors.Two rival views are described; the evide: The narrower conclusion keeps nothing of the abstract reading; it is a trimmed version of the revisionist one.
distractors.A view is described and its origins trac: The evidence won a 'victory'; it was not neglected.
distractors.A view is described together with an acc: The viols are mentioned only as a possibility the keyboard evidence cannot exclude.

questions.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that the author regards the "awkward passages" mentioned in the first paragraph as
choices: deliberate tests of the technical skill of keyboard players
the strongest evidence that the cycle was not intended to be performed
tasks that the composer left to performers rather than costs incurred for the sake of exposition
evidence that the composer did not try every combination of voices at the instrument
flaws that would disappear if the cycle were scored for a consort of viols

explanation.key: Paragraph 1 says the old reading excused the awkward passages 'as the price of demonstration'; paragraph 3 says the cycle's difficulties are 'not the residue of a demonstration but problems the composer expected performers to solve'. Linking the two gives the key.

distractors.deliberate tests of the technical skill: One notch too strong and too narrow: 'expected performers to solve' is not 'designed to test', and the author declines to limit the performers to keyboard players.
distractors.the strongest evidence that the cycle wa: This is how the old reading could have used them; the author holds that the cycle was meant to be sounded.
distractors.evidence that the composer did not try e: Unsupported; the passage says the hardest combinations fit two hands 'as though each had been tried'.
distractors.flaws that would disappear if the cycle: The viols appear only as another possible medium; nothing says they would remove the difficulties.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. According to the passage, which of the following was offered as evidence that the cycle was keyboard music?
choices: Nearly all of its voices lie within the range of a keyboard instrument of the time.
The composer is known to have tried each combination of voices at the keyboard before the cycle was printed.
The combinations of voices that are hardest to tell apart in print usually fit easily under two hands.

explanation.key: A: stated ('Nearly every voice lies within the compass of a keyboard of the period'). B: not stated; the passage says only 'as though each had been tried', a hedge, not a known fact. C: stated ('the combinations hardest to disentangle on the page almost always fall comfortably under two hands').

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the argument of the early-twentieth-century writers is best described as
choices: persuaded by its account of how the device arose, but doubtful that it captures the icons' devotional purpose
appreciative of its attention to what icons were for, but doubtful that it explains how the device arose
scornful of its reliance on theology at the expense of the evidence of the icons themselves
noncommittal, on the ground that the icons cannot settle whether the device was deliberate
admiring of its rigor, though uncertain whether the inconsistencies in the icons bear on it

explanation.key: The author calls the argument attractive, credits it with 'taking seriously what icons were for' and grants that the habit served devotion, but holds that the inconsistent convergences point to a workshop habit, not a deliberate theology of space.

distractors.persuaded by its account of how the devi: Reversed: the author accepts the devotional point and doubts the account of origin.
distractors.scornful of its reliance on theology at: Too strong; the author calls the argument attractive and grants its insight.
distractors.noncommittal, on the ground that the ico: Half-right: the author says the icons 'do little to confirm' the theory but takes a side ('more plausibly records a workshop habit').
distractors.admiring of its rigor, though uncertain: The author raises the inconsistencies as the main objection, and never praises the argument's rigor.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the workshop habit that the author proposes as an explanation for inverse perspective?
choices: A muralist reverses the vanishing point throughout a ceiling painting so that the figures appear to descend toward the viewers below.
A printer sets the hymns in a hymnal in unusually large type so that they can be read in a dimly lit church.
An apprentice who has been taught linear perspective applies it carelessly, so that the buildings in his street scenes converge toward different points.
A botanical illustrator draws a single plant showing its flower in profile and its leaves from above, a combination no one viewpoint could take in, so that each part can be identified.
A stage designer narrows the far end of a set so that a shallow stage appears deeper to the audience than it is.

explanation.key: The habit gives up a single coherent viewpoint so that each object can be shown in its most readable aspect. The illustrator does the same: no one viewpoint, but every part identifiable.

distractors.A muralist reverses the vanishing point: This matches the priests' theory (a consistent, deliberate inversion that opens the space toward the viewer), which the author doubts.
distractors.A printer sets the hymns in a hymnal in: Surface match on legibility and devotion, but nothing is sacrificed in the coherence of a depicted space.
distractors.An apprentice who has been taught linear: Surface match on inconsistent convergence, but it comes from carelessness, not from a habit serving legibility; it also assumes the system the author says painters did not know.
distractors.A stage designer narrows the far end of: An illusionist trick, the opposite of subordinating spatial illusion to legibility.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence in which the author grants a point that lends some support to the reasoning attributed to officials in the first paragraph.

explanation.key: The seventh sentence (An evacuation called too early does exact a price ...) grants that evacuating has a real cost, since a premature one can jeopardize the next; that is the officials' reasoning in the first paragraph, which weighed 'an evacuation whose costs were certain' against an uncertain warning. The fifth sentence's 'plausibly' concerns which agency should decide, not the officials' weighing of costs against uncertainty; the first sentence reports the reasoning but grants nothing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hazard maps drawn before several deadly eruptions correctly identified the towns that were later destroyed.
Uncertainty in volcanic forecasting has little bearing on whether officials decide to order evacuations.
Better instruments and models, rather than institutional reform, offer the surest way to prevent volcanic disasters.
Deadly failures to act on volcanic warnings have often had more to do with how responsibility for acting was divided than with the limits of scientific forecasting.
Officials who declined to order evacuations on the basis of uncertain forecasts were justified, since early evacuations are often undone.

explanation.key: The passage replaces the 'better science' account of unheeded warnings with an institutional one ('the decisive variable has often been institutional rather than scientific') while conceding that uncertainty matters.

distractors.Hazard maps drawn before several deadly: Too narrow: one piece of supporting evidence.
distractors.Uncertainty in volcanic forecasting has: Too strong: the author grants that a premature evacuation exacts a real price, so uncertainty matters.
distractors.Better instruments and models, rather th: Reversed: this is the view the passage disputes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
choices: The pool lowered its admission fee for the evening hours.
Swimmers who come in the evening tend to stay in the water longer than those who come in the afternoon.
Several other pools in the region extended their hours last year as well.
Before the change, nearly all rescues occurred during the crowded late-afternoon sessions, and many regular swimmers have since shifted to the far less crowded evening hours.
Attendance during the evening hours has been higher than the pool's managers expected.

explanation.key: Rescues were concentrated in crowded sessions; spreading swimmers into uncrowded evening hours raises total visits while thinning the crowds in which rescues happened. Both facts are explained.

distractors.The pool lowered its admission fee for t: Explains only the rise in visits, not the fall in rescues.
distractors.Swimmers who come in the evening tend to: More time in the water would, if anything, raise rescues, deepening the puzzle.
distractors.Attendance during the evening hours has: Again explains only the rise in visits.
